plain_english: The only people who truly have leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy. They are the only ones who really live. They don't just enjoy their own lifetime — they add every past century to their own. All the years that came before them belong to them too. Unless we're completely ungrateful, we should see these great thinkers — the founders of divine schools of thought — as having been born for us. They prepared life for us. Through their work, we can see beautiful truths that they brought from darkness into light. We aren't shut out from any time period. We can explore every subject. If we can find the mental strength to go beyond our human limitations, we have a vast amount of time to enjoy ourselves. We can argue with Socrates, question everything with Carneades, find peace with Epicurus, rise above human nature with the Stoics, or reject society with the Cynics. Since nature lets us commune with every age, why do we stay trapped in our own tiny, fleeting moment? Why not give our whole mind to what is vast, eternal, and shared with men better than ourselves?
original_excerpt: The only persons who are really at leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy: and they alone really live: for they do not merely enjoy their own lifetime, but they annex every century to their own: all the years which have passed before them belong to them. Unless we are the most ungrateful creatures in the world, we shall regard these noblest of men, the founders of divine schools of thought, as having been born for us, and having prepared life for us: we are led by the labour of others to behold most beautiful things which have been brought out of darkness into light; we are not shut out from any period, we can make our way into every subject, and, if only we can summon up sufficient strength of mind to overstep the narrow limit of human weakness, we have a vast extent of time wherein to disport ourselves: we may argue with Socrates, doubt with Carneades, repose with Epicurus, overcome human nature with the Stoics, out-herod it with the Cynics. Since Nature allows us to commune with every age, why do we not abstract ourselves from our own petty fleeting span of time, and give ourselves up with our whole mind to what is vast, what is eternal, what we share with better men than ourselves?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 14

plain_english: Think about those people who rush around all day making social calls. They exhaust themselves and everyone else. They go completely crazy with this routine — visiting every powerful person's house each day, never missing an open door. They take their fake, self-serving greetings from house to house, no matter how different these people are. But after all this effort in such a huge city full of people with such different interests, how many do they actually get to see? How many will be too lazy, too indulgent, or too rude to let them in? How many will pretend to be in a hurry and rush right past them after keeping them waiting forever? How many will avoid coming out to their crowded entrance hall and sneak out the back door instead? As if lying to a visitor isn't ruder than just turning him away! And how many are still half-asleep and stupid from last night's drinking? Even after someone whispers the visitor's name to them for the thousandth time, they can barely manage to grunt a greeting back to this poor man who woke up early just to wait around for them. All they can do is yawn with their mouth half-open — and it's insulting.
original_excerpt: Those who gad about in a round of calls, who worry themselves and others, after they have indulged their madness to the full, and crossed every patron's threshold daily, leaving no open door unentered, after they have hawked about their interested greetings in houses of the most various character,—after all, how few people are they able to see out of so vast a city, divided among so many different ruling passions: how many will be moved by sloth, self-indulgence, or rudeness to deny them admittance: how many, after they have long plagued them, will run past them with feigned hurry? how many will avoid coming out through their entrance-hall with its crowds of clients, and will escape by some concealed backdoor? as though it were not ruder to deceive their visitor than to deny him admittance!—how many, half asleep and stupid with yesterday's debauch, can hardly be brought to return the greeting of the wretched man who has broken his own rest in order to wait on that of another, even after his name has been whispered to them for the thousandth time, save by a most offensive yawn of his half-opened lips.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 14

plain_english: The people on the right track are those who spend time every day with the great thinkers — Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and all the other masters of wisdom, along with Aristotle and Theophrastus. None of these men will be too busy for you. None will send you away feeling worse than when you arrived. They'll always leave you happier and more at peace with yourself. They'll never let you walk away empty-handed. And here's the best part — anyone can enjoy their company, day or night.
original_excerpt: We may truly say that those men are pursuing the true path of duty, who wish every day to consort on the most familiar terms with Zeno, Pythagoras, Democritus, and the rest of those high priests of virtue, with Aristotle and with Theophrastus. None of these men will be "engaged," none of these will fail to send you away after visiting him in a happier frame of mind and on better terms with yourself, none of them will let you leave him empty-handed: yet their society may be enjoyed by all men, and by night as well as by day.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 14
